core_standard.paraphrase: Approve once a change clearly improves overall code health, even if imperfect; seek continuous improvement rather than perfection; never accept changes that definitely worsen code health except in a genuine emergency.
core_standard.heading: The Standard of Code Review

review_aspects.heading: Design
review_aspects.paraphrase: Most important item: do the pieces interact sensibly, does the change belong here, does it integrate with the system, is now the right time.

review_aspects.heading: Functionality
review_aspects.paraphrase: Does it do what the author intended and is that good for end-users and future developers; think about edge cases, concurrency, UI impact.

review_aspects.heading: Complexity
review_aspects.paraphrase: Check every level (line, function, class) for being hard to understand quickly or easy to misuse; watch for over-engineering for speculative future needs.

review_aspects.heading: Tests
review_aspects.paraphrase: Ask for appropriate unit/integration/e2e tests in the same change; check tests would fail when code breaks and are themselves maintainable.

review_aspects.heading: Naming
review_aspects.paraphrase: Names should fully convey purpose without becoming unreadably long.

review_aspects.heading: Comments
review_aspects.paraphrase: Comments should be clear, necessary and mostly explain why rather than what; prefer simplifying code over explaining it.

review_aspects.heading: Style
review_aspects.paraphrase: Follow the applicable style guide; mark non-guide preferences as Nit; keep large reformatting in a separate change.

review_aspects.heading: Consistency
review_aspects.paraphrase: Style guide requirements win; for recommendations, judge between guide and surrounding code; otherwise stay consistent with existing code and file cleanup bugs.

review_aspects.heading: Documentation
review_aspects.paraphrase: If build/test/use/release behaviour changes, related docs must be updated (or removed for deprecated code).

review_aspects.heading: Every Line
review_aspects.paraphrase: Read all human-written code assigned to you and understand it; if unqualified for an area (security, privacy, concurrency, a11y, i18n) ensure a qualified reviewer; note scope when reviewing only part ('Exceptions').

review_aspects.heading: Context
review_aspects.paraphrase: Look beyond the diff to the whole file and the whole system; reject changes that degrade code health.

review_aspects.heading: Good Things
review_aspects.paraphrase: Call out what was done well, as encouragement and mentoring.

review_navigation.paraphrase: Three steps: take a broad view (does the change make sense, good description?), examine the main part first and send major design comments immediately, then go through the rest in a sensible order (tests first can help).
review_navigation.heading: Navigating a CL in review

comment_labels.label: Nit
comment_labels.meaning_paraphrase: Minor polish point; technically should be done but low impact; author may choose to ignore.
comment_labels.heading: Label comment severity

comment_labels.label: Optional (or Consider)
comment_labels.meaning_paraphrase: Suggested as probably a good idea but not required.
comment_labels.heading: Label comment severity

comment_labels.label: FYI
comment_labels.meaning_paraphrase: Not expected in this change; information for the author to consider in future.
comment_labels.heading: Label comment severity

comment_principles.paraphrase: Be kind; comment on the code not the person; explain reasoning; balance pointing out problems with direct guidance (fixing is the author's job); prefer code clarification over explanations that live only in the review tool.
comment_principles.heading: How to write code review comments

cl_size_guidance.paraphrase: A change should be one self-contained change addressing one thing, including its related tests, and leave the system working. No hard limit: roughly 100 lines is usually reasonable and 1000 usually too large, and file spread also counts; reviewers may reject a change solely for size. Split by stacking, by files, horizontally (layers) or vertically (features); keep refactorings separate.
cl_size_guidance.heading: Small CLs / What is Small?

speed_guidance.paraphrase: Optimise for team velocity: respond shortly after a request unless mid focused task, and within at most one business day; individual response speed matters more than total review time; use LGTM-with-comments where appropriate; ask for large changes to be split; never trade review standards for imagined speed.
speed_guidance.heading: Speed of Code Reviews

cl_description_guidance.paraphrase: Description states what changes and why; first line is a short standalone imperative summary followed by a blank line; body gives context, trade-offs, links; avoid vague descriptions like 'Fix bug'; re-check the description before submitting.
cl_description_guidance.heading: Writing good CL descriptions

pushback_guidance.paraphrase: Consider whether the author is right; if not, explain further and politely persist where code health benefits; insist on cleanup now rather than later unless an emergency, filing a bug for unavoidable follow-ups.
pushback_guidance.heading: Handling pushback in code reviews

conflict_resolution.paraphrase: Seek consensus using the guide; move to a meeting/video call (record the outcome on the change); escalate to team, tech lead, maintainer or manager rather than letting the change stall.
conflict_resolution.heading: Resolving Conflicts

emergency_guidance.paraphrase: An emergency is a small change for e.g. preventing a launch rollback, a production bug badly affecting users, a pressing legal issue or a major security hole; soft deadlines, end-of-week pressure and rollbacks of test breakages are not emergencies; re-review thoroughly afterwards.
emergency_guidance.heading: Emergencies
